Su origen musical se discute: Mairena los tenía por cante básico gitano; los estudios recientes los llevan a Cuba y las habaneras llegadas a Sevilla y Cádiz en la segunda mitad del XIX; los granadinos defienden una raíz morisca (el disco Granada canta por tangos recoge trece estilos, entre ellos los de la morería). Manuel Ríos Ruiz concluye que no se sabe con certeza. La Niña de los Peines se hizo inmortal con su copla «Péinate tú con mis peines». Del tango nacen los tientos, más pausados y solemnes, que cantaron primero el Mellizo y el Marrurro y se popularizaron a comienzos del XX, y la mariana, que difundió Bernardo el de los Lobitos y hoy casi solo canta Pepe Menese con letras de Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: Las soleares
scenes.desc: La madre del cante y uno de sus pilares, independiente de cualquier otro ritmo; los cantaores la consideran «el toro bravo del arte jondo». Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los romances
scenes.desc: El flamenco distingue una docena de palos (romances, tonás, siguiriyas, soleares, tangos, cantiñas, cantes de Levante, fandangos, cantes de Málaga, ida y vuelta, aflamencados e híbridos), cada uno con sus estilos y sus creadores. Los básicos, los más antiguos, empiezan por el romance, la canción española más vieja transmitida oralmente, que los gitanos hicieron suya: es el verdadero punto de origen del cante. También llamados corridos, son las únicas coplas con continuidad narrativa (historias románticas, caballerescas o moriscas) y se cantan a palo seco, sin acompañamiento; con guitarra toman el son de la soleá por bulerías. Washington Irving los oyó en 1829 como «tonadas rudas y sencillas». Hoy casi no se cantan. José Blas Vega grabó en 1971 en el Puerto de Santa María dieciséis romances primitivos de siete intérpretes, todos gitanos, y los dividió en los de flores y Blancaflor, los carolingios, los del Cid, los de Bernardo el Carpio y los moriscos, como el de Zaide; su parentesco con tonás, carceleras, deblas y martinetes es evidente.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Name Change to Avoid Confusion (1966)
facts.body: In 1966, David Jones changed his name to David Bowie to prevent being confused with Davey Jones, the "cute little English dude" from the popular TV show, The Monkees. "In 1966, David Jones would change his name to David Bowie to avoid being confused with Davey Jones, who was the cute little English dude on the TV show The Monkeys."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Last Canadian and Touring Concerts (1966)
facts.body: The Beatles returned to Canada on August 17, 1966, for their final two concerts ever on Canadian soil in Toronto. This tour also marked the last time the band would ever play live, consisting of only eight shows over 12 days before they stopped touring forever to focus exclusively on studio music. "Just a year later in 1966, the band returned for their last two concerts ever on Canadian soil. The tour was also the last the band would ever play."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Canadian History Ehx"
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Final Toronto Concerts (1966)
facts.body: On August 17, 1966, The Beatles performed their last Canadian concerts in Toronto, with 15,000 fans attending the first show and 17,000 for the second at 8 pm. Bill J. Nelson served as MC, and the routine chaos continued, with 50 audience members treated for shock and screaming volumes making the music barely audible. "That number only went up to 17,000 fans for their second concert at 8pm."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Canadian History Ehx"
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Departure from Canada (1966)
facts.body: After their final concerts in Toronto on August 17, 1966, The Beatles stayed overnight before flying out to Boston on August 18th. This departure marked their definitive farewell to Canadian stages, as they never toured again. "This time, they left forever."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Canadian History Ehx"
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Post-1966 Studio Band Fades
facts.body: After 1966, when The Beatles stopped touring and evolved into a studio band, they frequently incorporated fade-outs into their songs. This allowed them to avoid crafting a definitive ending for a live audience, opting instead for an artistic or technical fade. "The Beatles were big into the fade after 1966 when they stopped touring and became a studio band and no longer had to properly finish a song for a live audience."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rock Explainer 3
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Early End to Touring (1966)
facts.body: Following the terrible sound experience at Shea Stadium in 1965, where they were miserable due to not being able to hear themselves, The Beatles played their last proper live gig a year later. The severe issues with concert sound reinforcement directly contributed to their decision to never tour again. "A year later, they played their last proper live gig, and they never toured again."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Concert Sound
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: "More Popular Than Jesus" Controversy (1966)
facts.body: In 1966, John Lennon's casual comment that The Beatles were "more popular than Jesus" ignited a significant controversy. Broadcasters Tommy Charles and Doug Layton in Birmingham, Alabama, initiated a campaign to ban The Beatles over this perceived blasphemy, leading to numerous records being broken and publicly burned. "And when John Lennon made a flippin' comment in 1966 about the Beatles being more popular than Jesus, two broadcasters, Tommy Charles and Doug Layton from Birmingham, Alabama, started a campaign to ban the Beatles over this blasphemy, and many records were broken and burned."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Invitation to Last Tour (1966)
facts.body: The Beatles invited The Ronettes to be their support act on their final tour in 1966. However, Phil Spector's insistence that Ronnie remain in the studio led to her cousin Elaine substituting, which reportedly disappointed The Beatles. "Also in 1966, the Runettes were invited by the Beatles to be their support act on their last ever tour, but once again Spectre insisted that Ronnie couldn't go because she needed to be in the studio, so Elaine substituted for her again, much to the Beatles' disappointment."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 110: "Be My Baby" by the Ronettes
facts.name: The Beatles

The severe issues with concert sound reinforcement directly contributed to their decision to never tour again. "A year later, they played their last proper live gig, and they never toured again."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Concert Sound
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Final Toronto Concerts (1966)
facts.body: On August 17, 1966, The Beatles performed their last Canadian concerts in Toronto, with 15,000 fans attending the first show and 17,000 for the second at 8 pm. Bill J. Nelson served as MC, and the routine chaos continued, with 50 audience members treated for shock and screaming volumes making the music barely audible. "That number only went up to 17,000 fans for their second concert at 8pm."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Canadian History Ehx"
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Invitation to Last Tour (1966)
facts.body: The Beatles invited The Ronettes to be their support act on their final tour in 1966. However, Phil Spector's insistence that Ronnie remain in the studio led to her cousin Elaine substituting, which reportedly disappointed The Beatles. "Also in 1966, the Runettes were invited by the Beatles to be their support act on their last ever tour, but once again Spectre insisted that Ronnie couldn't go because she needed to be in the studio, so Elaine substituted for her again, much to the Beatles' disappointment."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 110: "Be My Baby" by the Ronettes
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Last Canadian and Touring Concerts (1966)
facts.body: The Beatles returned to Canada on August 17, 1966, for their final two concerts ever on Canadian soil in Toronto. This tour also marked the last time the band would ever play live, consisting of only eight shows over 12 days before they stopped touring forever to focus exclusively on studio music. "Just a year later in 1966, the band returned for their last two concerts ever on Canadian soil. The tour was also the last the band would ever play."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Canadian History Ehx"
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Post-1966 Studio Band Fades
facts.body: After 1966, when The Beatles stopped touring and evolved into a studio band, they frequently incorporated fade-outs into their songs. This allowed them to avoid crafting a definitive ending for a live audience, opting instead for an artistic or technical fade. "The Beatles were big into the fade after 1966 when they stopped touring and became a studio band and no longer had to properly finish a song for a live audience."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rock Explainer 3
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: "More Popular Than Jesus" Controversy (1966)
facts.body: In 1966, John Lennon's casual comment that The Beatles were "more popular than Jesus" ignited a significant controversy. Broadcasters Tommy Charles and Doug Layton in Birmingham, Alabama, initiated a campaign to ban The Beatles over this perceived blasphemy, leading to numerous records being broken and publicly burned. "And when John Lennon made a flippin' comment in 1966 about the Beatles being more popular than Jesus, two broadcasters, Tommy Charles and Doug Layton from Birmingham, Alabama, started a campaign to ban the Beatles over this blasphemy, and many records were broken and burned."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Departure from Canada (1966)
facts.body: After their final concerts in Toronto on August 17, 1966, The Beatles stayed overnight before flying out to Boston on August 18th. This departure marked their definitive farewell to Canadian stages, as they never toured again. "This time, they left forever."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Canadian History Ehx"

facts.title: Early Lo-Fi Aesthetic (1966-1967)
facts.body: The band, composed of broke musicians associated with Andy Warhol, aimed to make a record with a meager budget of possibly $1,500. Their debut album, released in March 1967, was characterized by significant hiss, distortion, recording errors, a rough final mix, and poor stereo imaging, with singer Nico often being off-key. Despite these technical flaws, the primitive sound contributed to its appeal for a segment of music fans who valued authenticity and rebellion. "The Velvet Underground's records were generally derided for sounding bad, which made all kind of sense in the late 1960s and the early 1970s because the goal back then was to achieve perfect sound or something close to it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Lo-Fi: A History
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Cafe Bizarre Residency (Spring 1966)
facts.body: In the spring of 1966, the band began a residency at The Cafe Bizarre in Greenwich Village, New York, where their raw and gritty style attracted attention. "In the spring of 1966, they began a residency at a club called The Cafe Bazaar. This was in Greenwich Village."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Scepter Studios Demos (1966) – Discovered by Warren Hill
facts.body: On April 25, 1966, The Velvet Underground recorded demos at Scepter Studios in New York, resulting in two acetate test pressings that were circulated to record companies, all of whom declined to sign the band. The band later signed with Verve, re-recording their material. In 2002, Warren Hill found one of these acetates at a flea market in Chelsea, New York, for 75 cents. After researching its rarity, he auctioned it on eBay for $25,200, and it has since been digitized for wider listening. "What he had bought was one of only two copies of this test pressing. It featured the velvet underground recording some demos at Scepter Studios in New York on April 25th 1966."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Valuable Vinyl
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Featured in "Exploding Plastic Inevitable" (February-March 1966)
facts.body: The band's rehearsals, featuring Nico for the first time, were captured in Andy Warhol's iconic documentary "Exploding Plastic Inevitable," filmed around February-March 1966. During this period, Warhol incorporated many aesthetic elements that would become iconic for the band. "se grababa ese fantástico documental que yo creo que es icónico que es el explodimplastic inevitable de Andy Warhol en el que vemos todos estos ensayos de la velvita underground."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: The Velvet Underground: Una vision más humana que musical
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Unilaterally Designed Posters (1966)
facts.body: As early as 1966, Andy Warhol began designing and selling posters for The Velvet Underground completely unilaterally, without informing the band or showing them the designs. Band members would sometimes discover their own posters being sold after finishing concerts, having never seen them before. "Andy Warhol ya empieza a diseñar posters de la velvita underground, ya vendía primero en 1966 ya tenemos posters diseñados por Andy Warhol que se vendían sobre la banda, esto lo había hecho de manera totalmente unilateral sin ni siquiera avisar a la banda y sin ni si quieren enseñarles los posters que estaba vendiendo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: The Velvet Underground: Una vision más humana que musical
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Columbia Contract Debt (1966)
facts.body: By the time her Columbia contract expired in late 1966, Aretha Franklin actually owed the label money. This was a result of her string of low-charting, unprofitable singles and albums; she had recorded nine LPs for the label in six years, with more than half failing to chart and none peaking higher than number 69 on the Billboard album chart. "By the time that song peaked, not only had Franklin's Columbia contract expired, she actually owed the label money due to her string of low charting, unprofitable singles and albums."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Say a Little Prayer Edition Part 1
facts.name: Aretha Franklin

facts.title: Beatles' "Tomorrow Never Knows" (1966) – Blueprint for Psychedelic Music
facts.body: The Beatles' "Tomorrow Never Knows" from Revolver (1966) contains all the elements that defined early psychedelic music: drug references, an unusual rhythm track, sitar drone, backwards tape, sound effects, and samples. By 1966 the Beatles were deep into the drug culture that had lived in the jazz and folk world for years, incorporating their time in India with Maharishi Mahesh Yogi and their use of LSD. The Beach Boys' Pet Sounds (1966), Jefferson Airplane's "White Rabbit," the 13th Floor Elevators' album The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators, early Pink Floyd (including "Interstellar Overdrive," 1967), and the Velvet Underground (playing Andy Warhol happenings) all followed in this tradition. "That track has everything psychedelic music would need to get started."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: A Brief History of Alt Psychedelic Rock
facts.name: Psychedelic Rock

facts.title: Early Life and Abuse (1966-1980s)
facts.body: Born Sinead Marie Bernadette O'Connor in Dublin, she was the third of five children. Her mother, described as very strict and Catholic, frequently beat Sinead and her siblings, locking her in her room or a cupboard. This abuse, coupled with her mother's mental issues (leading to hospitalization after deliberately crashing a car), caused Sinead to rebel, skip school, and engage in shoplifting. "Mom was very strict in a scary, catholic sort of way, and often beat Shaneid in her siblings."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering Sinead O'Connor
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Hip-Pocket Records Releases (1966)
facts.body: Atlantic Records partnered with Filco and Ford in 1966 to release singles on Hip-Pocket Records. These thin, bendable plastic Flexi Discs were sold for $0.69 at Ford dealerships and Woolworth stores, featuring artists like Chuck Berry and Sonny and Cher. `"They got Atlantic, Mercury, and Roulette records to release singles this way, selling them for $0.69 at four dealerships and through Woolworth stores."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1
facts.name: Atlantic

"Capital records, the band's American record label, immediately recalled all 60,000 albums that had been sent out."

facts.title: Recall of "Butcher Cover" Album (1966)
facts.body: Capitol Records, The Beatles' American record label, immediately recalled all 60,000 copies of "Yesterday and Today" with the "Butcher Cover" that had been sent to stores in 1966, and held back an additional 750,000 records in warehouses due to the controversial artwork. "Capital records, the band's American record label, immediately recalled all 60,000 albums that had been sent out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Valuable Vinyl
facts.name: Capitol Records

facts.title: First Modern Concert T-Shirt (1966)
facts.body: The Grateful Dead pioneered the modern concert T-shirt with a design featuring their iconic skeleton-in-roses logo, created by Stanley Mouse in 1966. This marked a significant shift in perception, as selling merch was previously considered "uncool" and "too commercial." "And this has gone down in history as the first modern concert T-shirt, a grateful dead shirt."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rock Explainer
facts.name: The Grateful Dead

facts.title: Mike Davo Joins (1966)
facts.body: Mike Davo, formerly lead singer of A Band of Angels, eventually replaced Paul Jones. Jones himself unknowingly suggested Davo as a possible replacement, unaware he was already chosen. Manfred Mann recounted a silent drive to their last gig with Jones, where Dylan's "Just Like a Woman," their first single with Davo, played on the radio, highlighting the discomfort within the band. "Jones actually mentioned Davo to his bandmates as a possible replacement, not realising he was already in the group."

facts.title: Paul Jones' Departure (1966)
facts.body: Paul Jones announced his intention to quit the group concurrently with Mike Vickers' departure, but was persuaded to stay for nearly a year while a replacement was sought. Auditions with singers like Rod Stewart and Long John Baldry were unsuccessful. Relations between Jones and the rest of the group deteriorated to the point where they didn't inform him they were considering Mike Davo as his replacement. "But by the time that track was released, Paul Jones was out of the group. He actually announced his intention to quit the group at the same time that Mike Vickers left, but the group had persuaded him to stay on for almost a year while they looked for his replacement, or auditioning singers like Rudge Stewart and Long John Bouldery with little success."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Record Label Split and Career Concerns (1966)
facts.body: When Paul Jones left, the band faced a difficult situation as their record label decided to keep Jones as a solo performer. The rest of the group had to find another label and feared their career was over without Jones. "There was a lot of discomfort in the band at this time, because their record label had decided to stick with Jones as a solo performer, and the rest of the group had had to find another label, and were worried that without Jones their career was over."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: First Made-for-TV Pop Band (1966)
facts.body: The Monkees were assembled in late 1965 by ABC executives aiming to capitalize on The Beatles' success, making them the first made-for-TV pop band. Each half-hour sitcom-style show featured at least one music video-type sequence, leading to the band's rapid rise and a long string of hit singles. "The monkeys were the first made for TV pop band."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

facts.body: This album, released in 1966, is cited by some emo researchers as a starting point for emo music. This theory considers the record's lyrical themes, Brian Wilson's song construction, and his emotionally damaged state at the time of its creation as evidence for its early emo attributes. "some emo researchers, and there are such things, say that emo began with the beach boys and the pet sounds album in 1966, which is not really crazy if you look at the record's lyrical themes, how Brian Wilson constructed the songs, and the fact that he was so emotionally damaged at the time."

facts.body: This album, released in 1966, was described as a masterpiece that elevated Brian Wilson to the stature of a genius, carving an exciting new path for music alongside The Beatles' Rubber Soul. Before its release, The Beach Boys were known for adolescent hits about surfing, Californian girls, and cars. Inspired by Rubber Soul, Wilson created a deeply introspective and stimulating album, introducing orchestral arrangements and unusual sounds that challenged the pop and rock conventions of the time, with lyrics exploring profound themes like love, loss, and the search for meaning. "En 1966 vio la Luz Petzhounds de los Beach Boys, una obra maestra que lebo a Bryan Wilson a la altura de Gienio y Cabrío, junto con Raver Soul de los Beatles, un nuevo exitante camino para la música."
facts.source: Central Sonora

facts.title: Initial Music Cassette Failure (1966)
facts.body: In 1966, Philips introduced the first "musicassette" specifically intended for musical applications. facts.title: 50th Anniversary Box Set
facts.body: Released as part of a series of 50th-anniversary collections from 2017 through 2022 by Apple Records. The album was remastered by Giles Martin, son of the original producer George Martin, who deconstructed and reconstructed the album from the original master tapes to achieve a fresher sound with better stereo separation, aiming to sound as close to the original as possible. This box set, priced closer to $100, was particularly revelatory, offering insights like the morose origins of "Yellow Submarine." It is presented as a beautiful object, resembling a vinyl box with a large square shape, and includes a well-written book providing backstory on the band's career at the time. "This may have the most revelatory outtakes."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.body: At a show in Detroit in 1966, Pride confronted an audience that greeted him with silence upon realizing he was African American. facts.title: Factory Accident and Finger Injury (1966)
facts.body: At age 17, while working in a Birmingham factory that manufactured metal rings, Iommi suffered an industrial accident on his last day of work. Reassigned to a huge press that operated like a guillotine due to a colleague's absence, his right hand was caught, severing the ends of his middle and ring fingers. Doctors informed him he might as well forget about playing the guitar. "bang, it came down. It just took the ends off my fingers. I actually pulled them off."

facts.body: Intended as the perfect pop song and the first preview of Smile, its recording incurred a record cost of $50,000, the highest for a single track at the time. It was meticulously recorded in five different studios with up to 26 musicians, involving Wilson creating 28 variations of the verse and 37 of the chorus before selecting the best takes for the final version. The single, released on October 10, 1966, was a huge success, reaching number 1 in both the United States and England, and selling 400,000 copies in just four days. It was described as something "new and exciting," a psychedelic and hip-hop song in equal parts. facts.title: Founding by Dave Reeves (1966)
facts.body: Hiwatt, another British amplifier firm, was founded by electronic engineer Dave Reeves in 1966. His entry into amplifier manufacturing was serendipitous, beginning after he was laid off and used his severance pay to transition from repairing electronics to making them. "This one, founded by an electronic engineer named Dave Reeves. The best thing that ever happened to him was being laid off in 1966, with the severance money he moved from repairing electronics to making them."

The music industry and the public struggled to understand their atypical sound and imagery, leading to them being largely ignored, discarded, and forgotten for a period. "En 1966 publicaron Black Monk Time, su único disco, y lo que salió de ahí fue una mezcla de carias rock, distorsión obsesiva y letras que rozaban el daráismo político."

facts.title: Unreleased Project
facts.body: Brian Wilson conceived this project as an attempt to record the "best album in history," aiming to define the decade and expand music to new levels before The Beatles could. Following the success of Pet Sounds and "Good Vibrations," The Beach Boys reached an agreement with Capital Records for a release on January 15, 1967. However, after 10 months of intense work, the band was forced to cancel the album in May 1967, due to Brian Wilson's deep depressions, mental disorders, growing tensions within the band, and his increasing paranoia. Over 150 hours of recordings were archived. "Esta es la historia de Smile, el disco perdido que pudo cambiar la historia de la música."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: El Álbum Perdido que pudo cambiar la música ｜ Smile de The Beach Boys
facts.name: Smile

facts.title: Hip-Pocket Records Releases (1966)
facts.body: Roulette Records was among the labels that released singles on Hip-Pocket Records in 1966, collaborating with Filco and Ford. facts.body: Released by Andrew Loog Oldham, then manager of The Rolling Stones, this album featured orchestral instrumental arrangements of Stones songs for the easy-listening crowd. "In 1966, he released the Rolling Stones songbook under the name The Andrew Lou Geoldem Orchestra, and it featured this version of the 1965 Stone Song The Last Time."

facts.body: John Denver wrote this song, which became a number one hit for Peter, Paul and Mary in December 1969, their first and only number one hit. He demoed it under the working title "Babe I Hate to Go," and The Mitchell Trio later attempted it before producer Milton Okun gave it to Peter, Paul and Mary. Originally written about a lover's regret, the lyrics gained additional resonance by 1969, becoming a parable for soldiers leaving for the Vietnam War. "He'd even written a song that gave folk trio Peter Paul and Mary a number one hit."

facts.title: Written About Sunset Strip Riot at Pandora's Box Club; Sampled 36+ Times
facts.body: "For What It's Worth" was written about a riot that broke out to protest the closing of a Sunset Strip club called Pandora's Box in 1966. It remains one of the most popular 1960s counterculture songs and has been sampled at least three dozen times by artists including House of Pain, Everlast, Chumbawamba, and Butthole Surfers. It has been covered by everyone from Cher to David Cassidy to Ozzy Osbourne to Rush to Public Enemy to Stevie Nicks. "It remains one of the most popular 60s counterculture songs."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: A Brief History of Protest Music: Part 1
facts.name: For What It's Worth

facts.body: Originally intended to be titled "69 Tears," the band's record company intervened due to concerns that the number "69" carried offensive connotations. They persuaded the group to change the title to "96 Tears." "In 1966, they released a song that was supposed to be called 69 Tears, but fearing that the connotations of number 69 would offend people, their record company persuaded the group to make a change."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

facts.body: Nancy Sinatra's 1966 hit was featured in one of the most famous Scopatone films. Scopatones were video jukeboxes, weighing 1,500 pounds and capable of playing three dozen 16-millimeter films, most of which were in color and shot exclusively for the machine. "The most famous Scopatone movie featured Nancy Sinatra's 1966 hit, These Boots Are Made For Walking."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: This song was part of the loud music bombardment directed at the Branch Davidian cult compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993. It was one of the methods used by authorities to try and break the will of David Koresh and his followers during a 51-day standoff. "That playlist included AQ Breaking Heart by Billy Ray Cyrus, Nancy Sinatra, these boots are made for Wacan, some chanting by Tibetan monks, songs by Andy Williams, and some Christmas sing-alongs by Mitch Miller from the 1950s."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Using Music as a Weapon
facts.name: These Boots Are Made for Walkin'

facts.title: Transformative New York Trip (1966)
facts.body: In 1966, Schmidt traveled to New York, where he immersed himself in the experimental music scene, meeting and spending time with prominent figures such as Steve Reich, La Monte Young, Terry Riley, and even interacting with John Cage, feeling a deep affinity for their work. During his stay at the mythical and bohemian Chelsea Hotel, he also encountered Andy Warhol and his circle, including The Velvet Underground. "En 1966, un antiguo alumno alemán de Stochhaus en llamado Irmell Smith hace un viaje en Nueva York. Allí conoce y pasa tiempo con Steve Reitch, la Montellon, Terry Ridley e incluso llegó a tratar con John Cage. Sentía una gran afinidad hacia esos músicos. Se hospedan el mítico y bohemio del Chelsea, donde conoce Andy Warhol y a su entorno, incluía la velvete ante the Ground."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: CAN ｜ La Banda que (posiblemente) Inspiró a tu banda preferida
facts.name: Irmin Schmidt

facts.title: Infamous Butcher Cover
facts.body: An album issued in 1966 featuring original artwork of the Beatles posing with headless baby dolls and raw meat, known as the infamous "butcher cover." This photo, part of a collection by Robert Whitaker, was conceived as a protest against the Vietnam War and possibly a "dig" at EMI for "butchering" the Beatles' UK albums for North American release. A limited number of these albums were sent to stores, causing record store owners to be appalled. Capitol Records, the band's American label, immediately recalled all 60,000 albums distributed and held back another 750,000 in warehouses. A new cover was chosen, depicting the Beatles sitting around a steamer trunk looking annoyed. Many recalled albums simply had the new cover pasted over the old one, which could be carefully steamed off to reveal the original. A sealed copy of the original butcher version in mint condition can be worth $125,000. "In 1966, they issued the Beatles yesterday and today, an album where the original artwork featured the Beatles posing with some headless baby dolls in a bunch of raw meat."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Valuable Vinyl
facts.name: Yesterday and Today

facts.body: This song, one of The Beatles' most famous "kitty anthems," originally began as a morose composition by John Lennon that sounded "almost emo and sad." The box set outtakes allow listeners to literally hear the song evolving from its melancholic beginning into the fun, kid-friendly "Ringo Bop" it eventually became. It was primarily a Lennon-McCartney composition, with Ringo Starr performing the lead vocal. "You can literally hear them evolving, Yellow Submarine into the fun Kitty Ringo Bop that it became in the outtakes of this box set."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.body: Originally recorded in 1966, this song was one of three early hit singles for Neil Diamond on the Bang Record label. Initially, it struggled to get airplay in the States but eventually became a big hit in California. Diamond recounted pulling over in Toronto to listen when it came on the radio, feeling it was "the fulfillment of everything I ever wanted." Thirty-five years later, after four years of Freudian analysis, he realized he had written it about himself, as reflected in the autobiographical lyrics about seeking a partner who won't play games. "I was in Toronto and Solitary man had just been released. Nobody would play it in the States. But finally, it was played and became a big hit in California."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 41 - The Impact of The Troubadour on 1970s Popular Culture
facts.name: Solitary Man

facts.body: Originally intended by its writers to be "Semi-Detached Suburban Mr. Jones," the group changed the title to "Mr. James" to avoid any misinterpretation as an insult towards Paul Jones, who had recently left. This song, told from the perspective of a spurned lover insulting their ex's new fiancé, reached number two on the charts. "As the group felt that a song insulting semi-detached suburban Mr Jones, might be taken the wrong way. Lightly retangled, semi-detached suburban Mr James, made number two."

facts.title: Mental Health Strain
facts.body: Brian Wilson experienced a similar creative and mental health struggle after "Pet Sounds" (by The Beach Boys), which pushed him to the limits of his mental well-being. This illustrates the immense pressure that can accompany the creation of an unrepeatable work and the challenge of living up to or surpassing such an achievement. "Lo mismo le pasó a Brian Wilson traspet Sounds, sobre acomberé que el empujó al límite de su salud mental."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: El disco imposible: La historia de Loveless y My Bloody Valentine
facts.name: Pet Sounds

facts.title: Scepter Sessions Version
facts.body: A demo recorded by The Velvet Underground at Scepter Studios in New York on April 25, 1966. This particular version was part of a test pressing, with only two known copies ever circulated among record company executives, all of whom passed on signing the band. The band eventually signed with Verve and re-recorded their material, forgetting about these acetates. One copy was discovered by Warren Hill in a flea market box of records in New York for 75 cents in 2002, and later sold on eBay for $25,200, subsequently digitized for public access. "This is the Scepter Sessions version of Waiting for the Man."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Valuable Vinyl
facts.name: Waiting for the Man

facts.body: This 10-minute song, comprising six movements, was recorded for The Who's second album, *A Quick One*. It is credited to Pete Townshend and considered by some to be the first rock opera. "It's a 10-minute song containing six movements that was recorded for the who's second album called a quick one in 1966."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 42 - Rock Operas of the 70s
facts.name: A Quick One While He's Away

facts.body: This was one of three hit singles Neil Diamond recorded for the Bang Record label in 1966. "Neil Diamond recorded three songs, Solitary Man, Cherry Cherry, and I got the feeling. And that, my friends, was three hit singles for the Bang Record label."
